explanations.explanation: A farmer, friend. James says, "See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil." A farmer plants the seed and then has to wait, and he can't make a single sprout come up faster. I've stood over dough begging it to rise, so I know that feeling.

Shepherds show up all over the Bible, but James doesn't point to one here. He points to a farmer who awaits the precious fruit of the soil. The shepherd can sit this one out and keep an eye on his flock. This picture is all about crops and waiting.

A fisherman does a lot of waiting, I'll give him that. But James never mentions one in this passage. He says to see how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil, and that's the patience picture he gives the brothers.
Rains is the word. James says the farmer is patient for the fall and spring rains. Those are the rains his crop is waiting on. No rain, no harvest, and the farmer can't order it like a delivery.

Winds are a good guess, since the weather does a lot of the work out there. But James says the farmer is patient for the fall and spring rains. The rains are what the precious fruit of the soil is waiting on in this verse.
I'd be nervous about frost if I were a farmer, wouldn't you? But James doesn't mention it. He says the farmer is patient for the fall and spring rains, and that's what he's waiting on.

James says the opposite. He tells the brothers, "the Lord’s coming is near." He doesn't say it's a long way off, and he doesn't say when it will happen. He just tells them to be patient and strengthen their hearts.

False is right. James says, "You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near." So the patience he asks for comes with a reminder that the Lord's coming is near. I don't know the day, and James doesn't give one either.

True. James says, "Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged." Waiting can make people grumpy, and the grumbling lands on whoever is standing closest. James tells the brothers not to do it.

James does tell them not to. He says, "Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged." Waiting together can wear on people, and complaining about each other is the thing he warns against. The rule is right there in verse 9.

Judge. James says, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!" He says it right after telling the brothers not to complain about one another. It's a serious line, and the way he says it, you can tell he wants them to look up.
A King is a fine title and the Bible uses it for the Lord elsewhere. But in this verse James says, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!" The word he uses here is Judge.
A watchman stands guard at the door, so I see how you got there. But James says it's the Judge who is standing at the door. His words are, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!"

explanations.answer: The prophets who spoke in the Lord's name
explanations.explanation: The prophets. James says, "take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord." He calls them an example of patience in affliction. They spoke for the Lord, and James holds them up so the brothers can see what patient endurance looks like.

explanations.answer: The priests who served in the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests did serve in the temple, but James doesn't point to them here. He says, "take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord." The prophets are his example of patience in affliction.

explanations.answer: The kings who ruled over Israel
explanations.explanation: Kings are a big part of Israel's story, but James doesn't bring them up here. He holds up "the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord" as his example of patience in affliction. Nobody gets a crown in this verse.

Job is the man. James says, "You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord." Job is the one he names, and the brothers already know his name. James says the outcome came from the Lord.
Jonah, the prophet in the book of Jonah (Jonah 1:1), is a good name to know. But James doesn't mention him here. The man James names is Job, and he says, "You have heard of Job’s perseverance."
Samson, a judge in Israel (Judges 16:31), has some big stories. But James doesn't bring him up here. The man he names is Job, and he talks about Job's perseverance.

explanations.answer: He is full of compassion and mercy
explanations.explanation: That's it. James says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy." He says it right after pointing to Job's outcome from the Lord. Patient waiting isn't aimed at someone cold, and James wants the brothers to know that.

Scripture does say that God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29), but James doesn't say it here. After mentioning Job, he says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy." That's the line to hold onto in this passage.

explanations.answer: He tests those who love Him
explanations.explanation: James doesn't say that here. Right after Job, he says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy." Those are the words he leaves the brothers with in this verse.

Swear. James says, "Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath." He says "above all," so this one matters to him. The way he finishes the verse says a plain yes and no are all they need.
Boasting does come up in James's letter, but not in this verse. Here he says, "Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath." The word he uses is swear.

Arguing is a good thing to avoid, but it isn't what James says here. He says, "Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath." Swearing an oath is what he warns against.

James says the opposite. He tells them, "Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no, so that you will not fall under judgment." A plain yes and a plain no are enough, and no oath is needed to back them up.
False is right. James says, "Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no." So a plain yes or no is enough. If I say yes, I'd better mean yes, and the words don't need any extra decoration.

Sing praises. James says, "Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises." So the suffering person prays, and the cheerful person sings. I'd say pull out the loud voice for this one, because a happy heart has somewhere to send all that joy.
Rest is a lovely thing, but it isn't what James says here. He says, "Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises." The cheerful one is told to sing.

Helping the poor matters elsewhere in James's letter, but it isn't his answer in this verse. He says, "Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises." Singing praises is what the cheerful person is told to do.

The elders. James says, "He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The sick person calls them, and they come to pray. Nobody has to sit alone with it.
Deacons are named in the New Testament, but James doesn't mention them here. He says to call "the elders of the church." Those are the people the sick person calls.
Teachers are an important part of the church, but James doesn't name them here. He says the sick person should "call the elders of the church to pray over him." The elders are the ones he points to.
True. James says the elders should "pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The prayer and the oil happen together, and both are done in the name of the Lord.
James does say it. The elders are to "pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The oil and the prayer are both there in verse 14, and both are done in the Lord's name.

Restore. James says, "the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick." He follows it with, "The Lord will raise him up." It's all about the Lord doing the lifting, and nobody else gets the credit.
Comfort is a kind word, and I like it. But James says the prayer offered in faith "will restore the one who is sick." Restore is the word he uses.
Humble is a good word, but it isn't James's word here. He says, "the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick." Restore is what he says the prayer will do.
Forgiven. James says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." It comes right after the Lord raises up the sick one. I like it because forgiveness is the part you can't earn or buy at any price.
Rebuked sounds like a heavy answer, but James doesn't say it. He says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." That's the promise attached to the prayer.
A warning isn't what James says here. He says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." Forgiveness is what he promises.
James doesn't say that. He says, "The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail." He doesn't limit it to prophets. Then he gives Elijah as the example in the next verse.

False is right. James says, "The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail." It isn't only prophets who pray with great power. He backs it up in the very next verse with Elijah, a prophet he calls a man just like us (James 5:17).

That it would not rain. James says Elijah "prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years." That's a big prayer from a man James calls just like us. Elijah was a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 18:36).

explanations.answer: That the sun would stand still
explanations.explanation: The sun standing still was Joshua, Israel's leader after Moses, who spoke to the sun and moon in Joshua 10:12-13. That's a different man. James says Elijah prayed earnestly that it would not rain.
That's the sea Moses, Israel's leader, stretched his hand over in Exodus 14:21. But James is talking about Elijah, the prophet. He says Elijah prayed earnestly that it would not rain.
Years. James says it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. That's a long time to wait on the weather. And it all started with one man's earnest prayer.
Months would be long enough to make a farmer nervous. But James says it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. It's years, and that's the whole point of the number.
Weeks without rain would be dry, but James gives a much bigger number. He says it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. That's years, friend.

Crops. James says, "Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." After all that dry time, the rain came and the ground gave its crops. Elijah prayed, and the heavens answered.
Flowers would be a pretty ending, but James says something else. He says, "the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." Crops is the word.
Trees need rain too, but James doesn't name them. He says, "the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." Crops is what the earth gave.

That's it. James says, "Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins." Bringing a wandering brother back matters a great deal to him. It's a quiet thing to do, and James says it carries real weight.

explanations.answer: Earn a place among the elders
explanations.explanation: James doesn't talk about a title or a seat for the one who brings someone back. He says that person "will save his soul from death." The reward he names is bigger than a position.

James doesn't say it proves anything about the person who helps. He says whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way "will save his soul from death." His focus is on the one who gets brought back.
